newsitem.title: USA: Florida Keys wary of mangrove-munching monkeys.
newsitem.headline: Florida Keys wary of mangrove-munching monkeys.

text.p: Trudging through knee-deep muck and sidestepping monkey dung, a circuit court judge toured two islands in the Florida Keys this week to inspect damage inflicted by thousands of rhesus monkeys.

The islands, Lois Key on the Atlantic side of the island chain and Raccoon Key in the remote back country, have no human inhabitants and are owned by Charles River Laboratories. The Massachusetts-based company breeds rhesus monkeys on the islands and sells them to laboratories for medical research.

Environmentalists have waged a decade-long struggle to clean up the islands, which are littered with monkey waste and bare, sun-bleached mangrove trunks. The coastal mangroves' gnarled, sprawling roots provide a crucial habitat for young kingfishers, herons and egrets, but the monkeys like to strip the bark from the trees.

Circuit Court Judge Sandra Taylor inspected the islands to determine if the monkeys were being contained as stipulated in the terms of the company's agreement with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.
Under the 1988 agreement, the company was required to keep the monkeys cordoned off behind electric fences to facilitate a massive mangrove replanting effort.
The agreement also gave the company until 2008 to cage all the monkeys on Raccoon Key and until 2003 to cage those on Lois Key.
The Department of Environmental Protection, whose officials have inspected the islands, alleged the company had not lived up to the agreement.

Both sides agree that the monkeys have destroyed nearly all of the Red Mangroves that once ringed the islands. But Charles River officials said the task of replanting the trees and keeping the fiesty monkeys away from them has proved more difficult than anyone could have envisioned.
"We've done as good as we could under the circumstances," Charles River attorney Bill Roberts said.
He said the monkeys have learned to wade out into the water at low tide to get around the eletric fences meant to contain them.

Judge Taylor expects to rule on the matter in early August. If she finds that Charles River violated the agreement on the fencing issue, the company would have to accelerate the caging schedule for Raccoon Key by a decade. Most of the monkeys on Lois Key have already been caged.
Another Charles River attorney, Robert Routa, said the company was in "substantial compliance" with the agreement.
"You'll see a lot of damage out there," Routa warned as Taylor approched by boat. "But a lot of the damage was done when there were 6,000 animals out there in the early '80s."

The brownish-red rhesus monkeys weigh 35 to 40 pounds (16 to 18 kg) and are native to India and China. They have adapted well to the Keys but are not self-sufficient. A boat arrives daily to deliver fresh water and Purina Monkey Chow. The monkeys are skittish of their human caretakers and came no closer than 100 feet (30 metres) to the visiting judge and her party.

About 50 monkeys still roam free on Key Lois. The caging task will be trickier on Raccoon Key, which has nearly 1,000 free-roaming monkeys and is twice as large as Lois Key. At its peak in the 1980s, the 190-acre (76-hectare) island was home to more than 4,000 monkeys.
Although the timing is still unclear, both sides agree the monkey business on the islands will eventually cease. Charles River officials are scouting for a suitable alternative site.
